questions.prompt: A virus's RNA genome can be read directly by host ribosomes to make proteins. Its genome is:
questions.explanation: Positive-sense (sense) RNA acts like mRNA and can be translated directly.

questions.prompt: Which statement about negative-sense RNA viruses is FALSE?

options.text: Their genome must be transcribed into a + strand first.
Their genome can be translated directly into protein.
Their genome is complementary to positive-sense RNA.
Their genome is also called antisense RNA.
"Negative" has nothing to do with electrical charge.

questions.explanation: False. A −ssRNA genome can't be translated directly; it must be copied into + sense RNA first.

options.text: Makes RNA from a DNA template
Makes DNA from an RNA template

questions.explanation: It reverse-transcribes the retroviral ssRNA genome into dsDNA.

questions.prompt: After HIV's genome is converted to dsDNA, what happens next?

options.text: It integrates into the host chromosome as a provirus
It is translated directly by ribosomes
It leaves the cell by exocytosis
It is immediately packaged into new virions

questions.explanation: The dsDNA integrates as a provirus, which is then transcribed into new genomes and mRNAs.

questions.prompt: Why does a retroviral infection like HIV tend to be persistent?
questions.explanation: Its DNA copy integrates into the host chromosome as a provirus, which is copied whenever the cell divides and is hard for the immune system to detect. New viruses bud out slowly — few enough that the host cell can survive — so the virus stays at low, detectable levels for years.

questions.prompt: Influenza virus for vaccine production is grown cheaply and easily in:
questions.explanation: Embryonated eggs form a self-contained culture system — why flu shots ask about egg allergies.

questions.prompt: Which virus is most likely to require costly cultures of a specific human cell type?
questions.explanation: HIV only grows in specific human cells (CD4+ T cells), which must be cultured and passaged.

questions.prompt: Peyton Rous's 1911 chicken experiment resembled whose earlier method?

options.text: Ivanovsky's filtration of diseased tobacco plants

questions.explanation: Both passed diseased tissue through a filter and showed the cell-free filtrate caused disease (here, sarcoma).

questions.prompt: Which scientists first linked a virus to human cancer?
questions.explanation: Michael Anthony Epstein and Yvonne Barr — the Epstein-Barr virus, linked to lymphoma.

questions.prompt: Which statement about cell-cycle control genes is FALSE?

options.text: p53 mutations occur in about 60% of human cancers.
Proto-oncogenes encode proteins that turn on cell division.
p53 is a proto-oncogene that acts as the gas pedal.
p53 helps manage damaged and mutated DNA.
Tumor-suppressor genes encode proteins that turn off cell division.

questions.explanation: False. p53 is a tumor-suppressor gene — the brake, not the gas pedal.

questions.prompt: HPV and hepatitis B/C promote tumor formation mainly by:
questions.explanation: Viral proteins that inactivate p53 remove the brake on cell division.

questions.prompt: Explain how inactivating p53 can lead first to a tumor and then to cancer.
questions.explanation: p53 normally stops cell division and handles damaged DNA. Without it, cells keep cycling → uncontrolled growth (tumor). Because p53 also manages DNA damage, mutations accumulate and are passed on to daughter cells, turning uncontrolled growth into true cancer.

questions.prompt: What makes HeLa cells so valuable for research?

options.text: They are resistant to all viruses
They are immortal and divide indefinitely in culture

questions.explanation: Normal cells divide ~50 times in culture; HeLa cells keep dividing, giving a continuous cell line.

questions.prompt: Which genome type is replicated by host enzymes first making a complementary strand to form dsDNA?
questions.explanation: For ssDNA viruses, host enzymes synthesize the complementary strand, producing dsDNA that's then used like normal DNA.

questions.prompt: To replicate its genome, a +ssRNA virus such as a coronavirus must first make:
questions.explanation: The −strand copy serves as the template for producing many new +ssRNA genomes.

questions.prompt: Describe biosynthesis for a −ssRNA virus: how are proteins made and how is the genome replicated?
questions.explanation: The −ssRNA genome can't be translated, so a viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase first transcribes it into complementary +ssRNA. That +ssRNA is translated into viral proteins and also serves as the template for making new −ssRNA genomes.
